title: The golden lid
word: then two weeks of the peace chants
hook: a golden lid on the face of truth, and calm words about the body's end
carry: the self is not the body
tomorrow: a promise made in the future tense. does it get kept?

segments.voice: The peace chants and the closing mantras, day seven. Yesterday, Satyakama and satya: let your words match your mind. Today, not a door but an ending: the last lines of the Isha Upanishad.

Anywhere near the morning sun there's only glare. Whatever is out there, the brightness itself is what hides it. The Isha Upanishad ends on exactly that: the face of truth is covered by a golden lid. It's a short text, opened with purnam adah, and at its close the speaker stands before the sun and asks for the lid to come off. Many teachers, the great commentator Shankara among them, read these last lines as a prayer for the end of a life. They speak of it calmly, the way a traveler talks about the road.
screen: `ONLY GLARE.` → `A GOLDEN LID ON TRUTH'S FACE.` → `THE SPEAKER ASKS THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Here are the Isha's closing lines, in plain words. The face of truth is hidden by a golden lid. Pushan, uncover it, so that one who holds to truth may see. Pushan, lone seer, sun, spread out your rays and gather in your light, so I may see your most blessed form. That person there, I am that one. Then: let my breath go to the deathless wind, and this body end in ash. Mind, remember. Remember what was done. And last: Agni, god who knows every way, lead us by the good path. Notice what the speaker asks for. Not less light: the light gathered in, so the face behind it shows. And what's behind it? That person there, I am that one: the self shining in the sun is the self in the speaker. Then the plain facts: breath goes back to the wind, the body to ash. This is one of Hinduism's central teachings, the one Krishna gives Arjuna in the Gita: the self, the atman, is not the body, and is not slain when the body is. Many Hindus explain cremation the same way: the body is given back to fire and the elements, and the one who lived in it goes on. So the mind is asked to remember, and the fire is asked to lead.
screen: `A LID MADE OF GOLD.` · `THAT PERSON THERE, I AM THAT.` · `BREATH TO WIND, BODY TO ASH.` · `THE SELF IS NOT THE BODY.` · then, large: `LEAD US BY THE GOOD PATH.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, and if there's light on your face, from a window or a lamp, feel its warmth. Breathe out slowly and feel the breath leave you and become the room's air: breath to the wind. If you pray, say the Isha's last request softly: agne naya supatha, lead us by the good path. If you don't, say it in English. Then let each out-breath run a little longer, and rest there.
The peace chants and the closing mantras: today the Isha's last lines. The golden lid lifted, breath to the wind, and fire asked to lead by the good path.
For the road: the self is not the body. Breath goes to the wind, and the one who breathed goes on. Day done.

howItsDone: The Isha's closing verses are recited at the end of its study, and the last of them, the prayer to Agni to lead by the good path, is also said in other rites, including some said for the dying and the dead.

fork.setup: in a world religions class, someone asks why Hindus usually cremate. what fits the Isha's last lines?

fork.reveal: breath to the wind, body to ash: the Isha speaks of the body's end calmly, because the self is not the body. many Hindus explain cremation this way.

original.note: Sanskrit: by a golden vessel, or lid; the opening words of Isha 15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poetic sign-off.
what it means: a prayer to see past brightness to the self ('I am that one'), then calm words about breath and body going back, because the self is not the body.
what a scholar hears: Isha 15–18, also at Brihadaranyaka 5.15; Shankara reads them as a prayer at the end of life; the request is to gather in the light, not to dim it.
